title: What Happens to Your Customer Feedback Program When the Person Who Built It Leaves?
summary: When the person who built your customer feedback program leaves, it keeps running and quietly stops being true. Five steps to hand it over properly.
body_markdown:
Usually nothing visible, which is what makes it dangerous. The surveys keep going out, the digests land on schedule, and the dashboard still renders a number for the quarterly review. What left the building was the judgment underneath: why[the taxonomy is shaped the way it is](https://getthematic.com/insights/feedback-taxonomy-product-vs-journey) , which merges were considered and rejected, why one report quietly excludes a region, and which executive has never trusted that metric.


The direct answer: a feedback program survives its builder's departure to the degree that its decisions live in a system rather than in a person. Thematic holds the theme taxonomy, report logic, integrations, and permissions inside the platform rather than in one analyst's spreadsheets and bookmarks. That turns most of a handover into a question of access instead of reconstruction. The part no platform holds for you is the reasoning: why each theme means what it means, and why the numbers are cut the way they are. Write it down while the person who knows it is still engaged.


This isn't a rare event, and most teams[decide who owns the program](https://getthematic.com/insights/who-owns-voice-of-the-customer) once, at setup, then never revisit it. Median tenure in management, business, and financial operations occupations is[5.4 years](https://www.bls.gov/news.release/tenure.t06.htm) , according to the US Bureau of Labor Statistics. A feedback program older than about five years has already outlived the median tenure of the person who built it. Below are five steps to run well before anyone gives notice. If the change is a merger or reorg rather than one person leaving, see[how to merge two customer feedback programs](https://getthematic.com/insights/merge-two-feedback-programs) .


## The five-step process


1. **Inventory what only one person knows.** Find the decisions that exist nowhere but in someone's head.
2. **Write a definition for every theme, now rather than at handover.** A theme without a written meaning is one your successor will redefine by accident.
3. **Log who changed the taxonomy, when, and why.** The rationale matters more than the record.
4. **Move report logic and access out of personal accounts.** Anything tied to one login is a dependency.
5. **Distribute the relationships before you need to.** Stakeholder trust is the one asset you can't document.


## Step 1: Inventory what only one person knows


Software teams call this the bus factor: the minimum number of people who would have to disappear for a project to stall. A 2022 study based on[a survey of 269 engineers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.01523) found practitioners treat it as a real engineering problem, not a joke. Most feedback programs have a bus factor of one and have never measured it.


Write down the decisions that live nowhere but in someone's memory:


- Why a theme was split into sub-themes, and which merges were proposed and rejected.
- Why a recurring report filters out a market, a channel, or a date range.
- What changed at the last re-baseline, and which trend lines aren't comparable across it.
- Which stakeholders distrust which metric, and what they asked for instead.


A useful test: ask a colleague to reproduce last quarter's executive readout without asking the owner a single question. Whatever they can't do is your inventory. Remember too that[running the platform is four separate jobs](https://getthematic.com/insights/data-scientist-feedback-analytics-platform) , and they rarely all need to go to the same successor.


## Step 2: Write a definition for every theme, now rather than at handover


[Your theme taxonomy](https://getthematic.com/insights/how-to-build-a-customer-feedback-taxonomy) is a controlled vocabulary, and there's been a national standard for governing one since 2005. ANSI/NISO Z39.19 says a term should carry a scope note, and that[a scope note "should state the chosen meaning of a term"](https://groups.niso.org/higherlogic/ws/public/download/6484/Guidelines%20for%20the%20Construction,%20Format,%20and%20Management%20of%20Monolingual%20Controlled%20Vocabularies.pdf) and may also record the meanings deliberately excluded from it. That second half is the valuable one. "Delivery" means nothing on its own. "Delivery, covering courier handoff and delivery windows, excluding packaging damage, which sits under Product Condition" is a definition a successor can apply consistently.


Write these when the theme is created, not when someone resigns. Google's site reliability practice makes the same argument about runbooks:[whenever an alert is created, a corresponding playbook entry is created with it](https://sre.google/workbook/on-call/) . A handover document written in a two-week notice period, by someone who has already mentally moved on, is the weakest version of this.


In Thematic, the taxonomy lives in the Themes Editor rather than a local file, and "manage themes" is a named dataset permission, so you can see who is able to change it. The definitions are the part you still supply. ([Who owns the themes a vendor builds](https://getthematic.com/insights/who-owns-feedback-themes-taxonomy) from your data is a separate, contractual question.)


## Step 3: Log who changed the taxonomy, when, and why


Z39.19 is explicit that a term record "should note the date of each change and identify the individual responsible for it," and that a history note should track modifications by "recording previous forms with reasons for the change." The DDI Lifecycle metadata model, used by statistical agencies, makes the[rationale for a version change](https://docs.ddialliance.org/DDI-Lifecycle/3.3/model/item-types/StatisticalClassification/) a field in its own right, alongside a named unit responsible for the classification.


Rationale is the piece almost every program skips. Thematic's guidance already covers how to[version the taxonomy and keep a dated change log](https://getthematic.com/insights/keep-feedback-trend-lines-comparable) , and Revert Draft rolls back to any of the last three applied versions, showing who applied them and when. Three versions is a safety net, not an archive, so keep your own dated log alongside it with one line of reasoning per change.


The standard names the failure mode directly: when a term is modified or deleted, the impact on previously indexed records must be considered. When a new owner tidies a taxonomy they don't fully understand, every historical trend line silently stops meaning what it used to. Nothing errors. The chart still draws. The program doesn't visibly die, it quietly stops being true.


## Step 4: Move report logic and access out of personal accounts


Audit every output and ask what breaks when one login is disabled. In Thematic, dashboards, scheduled email digests, and alerting workflows are configured in the platform rather than in a personal calendar reminder, and each keeps its own execution history. Make sure[every recurring report has an owner](https://getthematic.com/insights/automate-customer-feedback-reporting) recorded against it.


Three things to check before anyone leaves:


- **Personal access tokens.** A token inherits the permissions of the user it belongs to and can be valid for up to three years. Any integration built on a departing person's token is a scheduled outage.
- **User deletion.** Deleting a user revokes access to the current organization, but it does not unsubscribe them from email digests. Remove them from subscriber lists separately.
- **Just-in-time provisioning.** JIT fires only on a user's first SSO login, so changing the default role later doesn't re-provision anyone who already has an account. Set a successor's permissions deliberately.


One gap to plan around: saved filter combinations in the analysis tools are kept as shareable links, and Thematic's advice is to store them with short descriptions in a separate document. Those really do live in one person's browser, so move them into that document first. Thematic has no feature that transfers a departing user's assets either, so make sure a second administrator already holds[the access and permissions](https://getthematic.com/insights/control-who-sees-customer-feedback) to manage anything that matters.


## Step 5: Distribute the relationships before you need to


Artifacts transfer. Standing is harder. A successor who inherits a perfectly documented program still has to earn the right to tell a skeptical VP their favorite theory isn't in the data.


The structural answer is to stop routing that credibility through one person. The XM Institute's model for CX program governance spreads it across[five defined roles](https://www.qualtrics.com/articles/customer-experience/five-elements-cx-program-governance/) : a core team, an executive sponsor, a steering committee, a working group, and a network of ambassadors. The practical version is less formal: bring the likely successor into[executive readouts](https://getthematic.com/insights/cx-dashboards-that-earn-executive-trust) a quarter early and let them present one section.


Forrester's US Customer Experience Index[fell to a new average low of 68.3 in 2025](https://www.forrester.com/report/average-us-cx-index-performance-falls-for-fourth-consecutive-year/RES186162) , a fourth consecutive annual decline, and named weaker employee experience first among the causes. A program whose usage has[spread beyond the insights team](https://getthematic.com/insights/feedback-analytics-adoption-after-launch) loses far less when one person goes.


## What this looks like in practice


One e-commerce retailer ran its NPS program the way most do at first. The Director of Operations personally read the open-ended comments and classified them by hand, and as the company put it, the onus was on one individual alone. After moving to Thematic, a named representative in each team reviewed feedback monthly instead. The analysis stopped depending on one person, which is the change a good handover forces anyway, made deliberately rather than under pressure.


A large financial services provider shows the taxonomy half. Working from under a hundred survey responses a month, the team built one compact, tuned theme set that became the shared language for NPS across the business, and over the program NPS improved by more than 20 points, moving from negative to positive. A shared taxonomy is a company asset, not a personal one, so whoever reads the feedback next inherits the same definitions.


## Common mistakes to avoid


- **Treating the handover as a document written in the final two weeks.** By then the author is disengaged and the reasoning is already fading.
- **Logging what changed without logging why.** "Merged Delivery and Shipping" tells a successor nothing about whether to keep the merge.
- **Letting the new owner tidy the taxonomy in their first month.** It's the most natural instinct and the fastest way to break every trend line. Make structural edits in batches, with a written reason and a re-baseline plan.
- **Assuming deprovisioning is complete because the account is gone.** Tokens, digest subscriptions, and inherited integrations outlive the login.
- **Confusing documentation with distribution.** A perfectly documented program with one user still has a bus factor of one.


## The short answer


The program keeps running and slowly stops being trustworthy, because the reasoning behind the themes and the reports left with the person who held it. The fix isn't a better exit interview. It's writing a definition for every theme, logging the reason behind every taxonomy change, keeping report logic and access in the platform rather than in personal accounts, and making sure more than one person has standing with the stakeholders who act on the results.
